title: Supplemental Technical Comments of Christian C. Nzeanorue concerning the timely, orderly, and reliable interconnection of large loads to the interstate transmission system under RM26-4.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
BEFORE THE
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System
Docket No. RM26-4-000

SUPPLEMENTAL TECHNICAL COMMENTS OF CHRISTIAN CHUKWUEMEKA
NZEANORUE
I. INTRODUCTION

I am submitting these supplemental technical comments in Docket No. RM26-4-000 concerning
the timely, orderly, and reliable interconnection of large loads to the interstate transmission system

I am an electrical engineer and researcher working in the areas of power system modeling, dynamic
stability, and grid reliability. My professional work includes dynamic and steady state reliability
analysis, generator model validation, stability studies, and the development of computational tools
supporting power system engineering workflows. Alongside this work, my research focuses on
advancing predictive stability and operational risk assessment methodologies that account for the
changing behavior of inverter-based resources and rapidly growing computational and industrial
loads. My broader objective is to support the reliability, resilience, and operational security of the
U.S. electric grid as these resources become increasingly significant to power system planning and
operations

I submit these comments solely in my individual capacity. The opinions contained herein are my
own and do not reflect the opinions of my employer or any other organizations to which I may
belong.

The Commission is considering how large loads can connect to the transmission system more
efficiently while maintaining reliability. Among the issues identified by the Commission are
whether large loads and co located facilities that agree to be flexible and curtail usage should be
able to move through interconnection studies faster, how such a process should work, whether
studies could be completed within 60 days, and how grid reliability should be evaluated when an
existing generating facility partially shuts down to serve a new large customer at the same
location.[1]

These issues pose a significant engineering question. The question for accelerated interconnection
should not just be whether a proposed load is above a certain MW limit, but whether its
characteristics, electrical location, operating behavior and interaction with the surrounding
transmission system generate reliability situations that need additional analysis.

I therefore recommend that the Commission ask RTOs, ISOs and transmission providers to employ
a structured technical screening process to decide how far to go in studying large load
interconnections.
 Stage 1: Model and Data Readiness

Determine whether sufficient technical information exists to represent the proposed facility for the
analyses that may be required.

Stage 2: Initial Reliability Screening

Evaluate characteristics that may increase the complexity or potential reliability impact of the
interconnection.

Stage 3: Proportionate Study Path

Use the screening results to determine whether the facility is suitable for an accelerated assessment
or whether targeted additional analysis is warranted.

Stage 4: Post Commissioning Validation
If material study assumptions impact reliability conclusions, compare the assumptions with
commissioning or operational information and update models where necessary.

This framework would not supersede existing reliability requirements nor mandate the same
studies in all regions. Instead, it would give a practical tool to decide when expedient treatment is
technically appropriate and when further engineering analysis is warranted.

II. A 60 DAY STUDY TARGET SHOULD BE CONDITIONED ON TECHNICAL
READINESS AND RELIABILITY COMPLEXITY

The Commission is seeking stakeholder input on whether large loads and co-located facilities that
agree to be flexible and curtail usage should be able to move through interconnection studies faster,
how such a process should work, and whether studies could be completed within 60 days.[2]

For qualifying projects, a 60-day target may be reasonable if two conditions are met.

Firstly, the applicant should provide sufficient technical information to enable the required
reliability assessment to be made.

Second, a preliminary screening should indicate that the proposed interconnection does not have
any reliability conditions that would require further investigation.

The study timeline should therefore not be used to define the technical scope of the assessment but
rather follow the technical scope of the assessment.

For example, an interconnection with full technical information, well documented operating
characteristics, documented and proven curtailment capacity and limited known system
sensitivities, might be considered for accelerated treatment.

Conversely, if initial screening indicates that the voltage, frequency, transient stability, protection
or other reliability issues are potentially material, then the process should allow for further
analysis, even if it takes longer than the accelerated target.
 This would ensure that the defined study timeframe would not be restricted due to an
administrative timeframe and the engineering analysis would be completed in the defined study
timeframe.

III. THE COMMISSION SHOULD ENCOURAGE A STRUCTURED RELIABILITY
SCREENING FRAMEWORK

The Commission should encourage transmission providers to establish transparent technical
screening criteria for determining study depth.
The screening process should be proportionate and regionally adaptable. It should not require
every large load to undergo the same level of analysis.
The screening process could at least consider the following categories if applicable to the proposed
facility and surrounding system.
A. Facility Characteristics
Relevant characteristics can be:

   1. Requested withdrawal magnitude and expected load growth.
   2. Concentration of demand at the point of interconnection.
   3. Load composition.
   4. Expected ramping characteristics.
   5. Potential for rapid or simultaneous load reduction.
   6. Power electronic interfaces.
   7. On site generation or energy storage.
   8. Uninterruptible power supply systems.
   9. Material protection and control characteristics.
   10. Curtailment and restoration behavior.

B. Electrical Location

Proposed point of interconnection and transmission system characteristics should also be taken
into account for screening, such as:

   1.   Relevant transmission constraints.
   2.   Voltage sensitivity.
   3.   Available reactive support.
   4.   Credible contingencies.
   5.   System strength where relevant.
   6.   Nearby generation characteristics.
   7.   Other identified local or regional system sensitivities.

C. Operating Characteristics
The assessment should include an evaluation of whether the facility has operating characteristics
that would materially affect the conditions of the system such as high demand rate of change,
 correlated demand behavior, high demand restoration ramps, or controls that could materially
affect net demand.

D. Flexibility Characteristics

If expedited treatment requires curtailment or other load flexibility, the screening process should
identify whether the capability can be modeled and used for planning and operations.

These categories are not meant to establish a national "checklist". There are significant variations
in the topology, operating conditions, planning practices, and reliability constraints of regional
systems. Instead, these categories offer a standardized engineering framework for each
transmission provider to decide on the study path to follow for a given material, depending on the
reliability characteristics of the material.

IV. SCREENING RESULTS SHOULD DETERMINE THE STUDY PATH
The screening process should lead to an identifiable study path.
I recommend considering a three-level structure.

Path 1: Accelerated Assessment

A project can be advanced to an accelerated assessment where the technical information is
adequate, and screening has determined that there is no material condition that needs to be analyzed
in detail.

This pathway could help the Commission reach its goal of quicker interconnection and could
potentially be in line with the proposed 60-day target.
Path 2: Targeted Additional Assessment

If a specific sensitivity is identified through screening, further analysis should be directed to that
sensitivity instead of automatically sending the project through all the available studies.

For instance, a project with material voltage sensitivity might need further voltage study and a
plant with fast load reduction or restoration characteristics might need specific dynamic study.
This way, additional research is focused on the reliability concern, while maintaining efficiency.

Path 3: Detailed Reliability Assessment

If screening reveals more than one or potentially significant system interaction, a more extensive
assessment might be warranted.

This may involve extra steady state, short circuit, transient stability, voltage stability, frequency,
electromagnetic transient, protection or other analysis as necessary for the specific system and
facility.
Study depth should progress in proportion to technical complexity demonstrated and not just
facility size.
 This would enable transmission providers to focus engineering resources in the areas where they
would be most useful to increase reliability value, and to expedite lower complexity projects.

V. MODEL AND             DATA     READINESS         SHOULD       PRECEDE ACCELERATED
TREATMENT

Reliable study results depend on appropriate technical representations of the proposed facility.

NERC's approved Reliability Guideline: Risk Mitigation for Emerging Large Loads explains that
appropriate large load data are foundational to reliable planning and operations and describes data
collection across three stages: interconnection evaluation, integration and commissioning, and
operations.[3]
The guideline also acknowledges that planners may require steady state and dynamic data adequate
to accurately model large load facilities in reliability studies.[4]
These developments support an important principle for accelerated interconnection:
Model and Data readiness should be part of study readiness. However, it does not necessarily imply
that each facility must have the most detailed model possible at the start of the process.
The necessary information should, rather, be proportional to the required analysis. Conventional
representations might be sufficient for relatively simple facilities. Systems with large amounts of
power electronic conversion, significant changes in demand, complex control characteristics, high
on-site generation or storage, or other factors that impact system response may need more detail.

A study done quickly with incomplete or materially inaccurate assumptions may result in false
efficiency if the assumptions subsequently need to be restudied, the model subsequently needs to
be corrected, commissioning changes are required, or operational restrictions are necessary.

Accordingly, completeness and fitness of technical data should be considered when determining
eligibility for accelerated treatment.

VI. REPRESENTATIVE SCENARIO ANALYSIS SHOULD BE                                    USED WHEN
SCREENING IDENTIFIES MATERIAL SENSITIVITY

Reliability impacts of large loads may vary with system conditions. A facility that operates well in
one topology and dispatch condition may behave differently in another relevant topology and
dispatch condition.

If during the initial screening, material sensitivity is identified, the study process should then
consider a manageable number of representative scenarios.

The objective should not be to simulate every conceivable operating condition.
Transmission providers, rather, should identify scenarios that can show the conditions of the
transmission system most pertinent to the concern.

These can vary by facility and system and may include:
   1. Seasonal or load level conditions.
    2.   Relevant generation dispatch patterns.
   3.   Transmission outages.
   4.   Credible contingencies.
   5.   Variations in reactive power availability.
   6.   Changes in system strength where relevant.
   7.   Varying output from inverter-based resources where material.
   8.   Credible rapid load reduction or restoration events.
   9.   Other operating configurations associated with identified sensitivities.

This can help to enhance efficiency and reliability.

Less sensitive conditions can be screened without the need for detailed analysis, and engineering
resources can be focused on those conditions that are best able to elicit significant system
responses.
VII. CURTAILMENT SHOULD BE DEFINED AS A MEASURABLE ENGINEERING
CAPABILITY
The Commission is specifically seeking input on whether large loads and co located facilities that
agree to flexibility and curtailment should receive faster interconnection treatment.[5].
From an engineering point of view, a commitment to curtail is most useful if it can be translated
into measurable operating characteristics.

Relevant characteristics may include where curtailment is used to enable expedited treatment or to
avoid a reliability limitation:

   1.   Available MW reduction.
   2.   Response time.
   3.   Duration.
   4.   Control or dispatch mechanism.
   5.   Communications capability.
   6.   Telemetry.
   7.   Availability under relevant system conditions.
   8.   Restoration behavior.
   9.   Procedures for verifying performance.

This would allow flexibility to be represented appropriately in planning and operational studies. It
would also differentiate a contractual obligation to reduce from a technically defined capability
that can reasonably be included in reliability assessments by system operators.

If the expedient treatment relies on curtailment as a material basis, the capability assumed should
thus be documented and verifiable.
 VIII. NET MW SHOULD NOT BE THE SOLE RELIABILITY CONSIDERATION FOR
CO LOCATED GENERATION AND LARGE LOADS

The Commission is also seeking input on how grid reliability should be evaluated when an existing
power plant seeks to partially shut down to serve a new large customer at the same location,
including whether future load growth should be considered and whether required grid upgrades
should be completed first.[6]

Net injection or withdrawal at the point of interconnection is important, but it should not
necessarily be the only technical consideration. There can be two configurations that give the same
net MW transfer but have different electrical or dynamic characteristics. With a new large load and
a change in generation operation, depending on the specific generating facility, the characteristics
that are important to voltage performance, reactive capability, frequency response, short circuit
performance, protection performance, or disturbance response, may change.
Therefore, the reliability assessment should consider material changes in the power transfer and
system performance characteristics.
Considering future system conditions is also technically appropriate. A reliability conclusion
should consider reasonably anticipated system conditions over the study horizon of interest and
not just the system configuration at the time of the request.

The timing of the generation change and large load service should be coordinated with the timing
of the upgrades or other mitigation measures identified by the reliability assessment that are needed
to maintain applicable reliability performance under the proposed operating configuration. This
would enable sequencing to be based on the reliability identified and not on the same prerequisite
for all co-located arrangements.

IX. POST COMMISSIONING VALIDATION SHOULD CLOSE THE LOOP BETWEEN
STUDIES AND OPERATIONS
Interconnection studies necessarily rely on information available before a facility becomes fully
operational
NERC's approved large load reliability guideline describes data collection and modeling as a
lifecycle process extending from interconnection evaluation through integration and
commissioning and into operations.[7]

The 2026 aggregated industry report from NERC revealed that there were gaps in existing
practices. Among other things, NERC found that the majority of responding entities had no
processes that involved large loads updating the modelling data after design changes, upgrades or
model validation based on disturbances. NERC also reported that entities with commissioning
practices generally did not include model verification or model validation to support Bulk Power
System reliability.[8]
These findings contribute to practical life cycle approach. If a reliability conclusion is materially
dependent on a characteristic of a facility, then the characteristic should be one that can be
compared with information obtained during the commissioning or early operation of the facility.
 Some of the relevant characteristics might be:

   1.   Ramping behavior.
   2.   Curtailment response.
   3.   Restoration behavior.
   4.   Disturbance response.
   5.   Material protection or control behavior.
   6.   Other characteristics specifically relied upon in the interconnection assessment

If there are any significant discrepancies between observed behavior and the assumptions made in
the study, pertinent technical information and models should be revised and further evaluation
should be considered.

This forms a practical engineering process:

Model and Data Preparation => Reliability Screening => Appropriate Study => Commissioning
=> Validation => Model Update When Necessary

This process would enhance the interconnection studies, planning models and operational
information continuity.

X. THE PROPOSED FRAMEWORK COMPLEMENTS ONGOING NERC AND FERC
LARGE LOAD INITIATIVES

The recommendations in these comments are not to be read as an alternative to NERC's work on
emerging large loads.

NERC has already undertaken substantial activity concerning large load data, modeling,
validation, commissioning, planning and operational studies, disturbance performance, and
computational loads.[9]

The framework proposed here tackles a more limited implementation question:

How should transmission providers determine when accelerated interconnection is technically
appropriate and when additional reliability analysis is warranted?

A structured screening and study path can provide that bridge.

NERC can continue to advance reliability practices and requirements, and transmission providers
can apply clear screening criteria to help identify the depth of analysis to be applied during the
interconnection process.
This also fits in with the Commission's more recent recognition of regional differences.

On June 18, 2026, FERC initiated separate proceedings with the six regional grid operators and
their transmission owners. The Commission stated that the orders were intended to consider
regional variations in the current study process, transmission service models, planning
responsibilities, cost transparency, network upgrades, and other factors related to the integration
of large loads. The Commission also allowed each RTO and ISO to establish their own definition
of large loads and operational requirements specific to their region.[10]
 The Commission is therefore able to establish common principles of technical readiness,
proportionality, transparency and validation and give regional entities flexibility in implementation
details.

XI. RESPONSE TO THE PRINCIPAL TECHNICAL QUESTIONS IDENTIFIED BY THE
COMMISSION

To clarify, here are my answers to the principal technical questions relevant to these comments.

A. Should studies for flexible and curtailable large loads and qualifying co-located facilities
be expedited?

Yes, if sufficient technical data are available and a preliminary reliability screening suggests that
the facility will be appropriate for accelerated assessment. Additional analysis should not be
precluded by expedited treatment if material reliability concerns are identified.
B. Can an expedited study be completed within 60 days?
A 60-day target may be achievable for qualifying projects, but it should not operate as an absolute
technical limit. The timeline should be based on the readiness of the model and data, system
sensitivities identified and the scope of analysis reasonably necessary to evaluate reliability.

C. How should curtailment be considered?
Curtailment should be expressed as an observable and quantifiable operating capacity. If a
reliability conclusion is based on curtailment, the following assumptions regarding magnitude,
response time, duration, communications, availability and restoration should be documented.

D. How should reliability be evaluated when existing generation partially shuts down to serve
a new large load?

Both power transfer and the changes in electrical and dynamic system characteristics should be
assessed. Net MW may not reflect changes which are relevant to voltage, frequency, reactive
capability, protection or disturbance response.

E. Should future system conditions be considered?

Yes.

The study should take into account reasonably expected system conditions during the time period
under study, such as projected load growth and other significant changes that may impact the
reliability determination.

F. How should new requirements apply to large-load interconnection requests already under
review?

Completed studies should not automatically be required to be restarted because of a new
framework pending requests. If the reliability study is incomplete because of the characteristics of
the material used in the proposed facility or assumptions made for the system, or if material
characteristics of the proposed facility or system assumptions have changed since the time of the
 reliability study, the request could be screened under the applicable technical criteria to decide
whether supplemental reliability analysis is warranted. This would help in the transition to the new
framework, while avoiding needless repetition of technically sufficient studies that have already
been carried out.
XII. CONCLUSION

The Commission has a chance to speed up the interconnection of large loads without sacrificing
the technical rigor that is needed to ensure reliable operation of the interstate transmission system.
Those objectives need not conflict. A structured framework for reliability screening can help to
accelerate the process for relatively simple projects and to focus in-depth engineering analysis on
facilities and system conditions that are more likely to require detailed analysis.

Accordingly, I recommend that the Commission consider the following principles:
   1. Model and data readiness should be considered when determining eligibility for accelerated
      treatment.
   2. Initial reliability screening should determine study depth.
   3. A 60-day study target should apply to qualifying projects without preventing additional
      analysis when material reliability concerns are identified.
   4. Additional studies should be targeted to identified system sensitivities rather than applied
      uniformly.
   5. Curtailment and flexibility assumptions relied upon for reliability should be measurable
      and verifiable.
   6. Co-located generation and load arrangements should be evaluated based on material
      electrical and dynamic characteristics in addition to net power transfer.
   7. Material assumptions should be compared with commissioning or operational information
      where appropriate.
   8. The Commission should establish common principles while preserving sufficient regional
      flexibility for implementation.

This approach would offer a practical relationship between accelerated interconnection and the
reliability practices which are becoming more important as large, complex loads are added to the
transmission system.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments.



Respectfully submitted,
Christian Chukwuemeka Nzeanorue
Electrical Engineer Researcher in Power System Stability and Reliability Risk Assessment
